keyPoints: Separate package evidence from service health

slides.narration:
A server is missing one utility. An administrator downloads a binary from an unfamiliar website, copies it over a packaged executable, and forgets the change. Months later, nobody can explain why the host behaves differently from its peers. Package management exists partly to prevent this loss of provenance.

A package is not only a compressed program. It participates in a system of ownership, dependencies, trusted sources, configuration, updates, and removal. This chapter shows how to use that system without treating a successful installation as the end of operational responsibility.

slides.title: 6.1 Linux Packages
keyPoints: A software package bundles files and metadata such as name, version, architecture, dependencies, and installation actions. Package metadata lets an administrator ask which software owns a file and what should change during an update.

slides.narration:
A software package bundles files and metadata such as name, version, architecture, dependencies, and installation actions. Package metadata lets an administrator ask which software owns a file and what should change during an update.

Packages may include service units, users, directories, and scripts run during installation or removal. Therefore installing a package is a privileged change, not simply unpacking bytes. Review the proposed transaction, especially when it includes removals or new services.

A package version can include distribution-specific release information. Compare the complete version and vendor advisory context rather than only the upstream number. Enterprise distributions can backport fixes, so an older-looking upstream version is not by itself proof that a known vulnerability remains unpatched.

slides.title: 6.2 Software Repositories
keyPoints: Linux example — 6.2
Inspect package sources without refreshing them.
What to check: Enabled sources should belong to the intended release and trust policy.
slides.narration:
A repository is a managed source of packages and metadata. The package manager uses its metadata to discover versions and dependencies. Repository trust depends on configured signing keys, metadata verification, transport, and the publisher’s release process.

Transport encryption and package signing solve different problems. HTTPS protects a connection to a server; signature verification helps establish the provenance of signed metadata or packages. Neither proves that the software is appropriate for your workload.

Keep enabled repositories intentional and documented. An extra repository can affect future dependency resolution even when you installed only one package from it today. Record its owner, purpose, signing-key source, supported releases, and removal plan.

slides.title: 6.3 RPM
keyPoints: RPM is a package format and lower-level package-management tool used in the RHEL and SUSE families. It can query installed packages, list owned files, and verify selected metadata.

keyPoints: DNF resolves dependencies and manages packages from configured repositories. Typical operations include search, information, installation, removal, updates, and transaction history.
Review the transaction before accepting it. For automated changes, an unattended confirmation flag is appropriate only after the package set, repositories, and acceptance criteria are controlled.
Linux example — 6.4
slides.narration:
DNF resolves dependencies and manages packages from configured repositories. Typical operations include search, information, installation, removal, updates, and transaction history.

Review the transaction before accepting it. For automated changes, an unattended confirmation flag is appropriate only after the package set, repositories, and acceptance criteria are controlled.

DNF transaction history helps reconstruct what changed, but history undo is not a universal rollback. Older packages may no longer be available, script effects may not be reversible, and application data may have changed format. A reliable rollback plan includes compatible packages, configuration, and data state. (R12)

slides.narration:
APT manages DEB-based systems using repository metadata. apt update refreshes package lists; it does not upgrade installed software. apt upgrade applies eligible upgrades under its documented constraints, while more expansive operations can alter the package set more substantially.

apt policy helps identify installed and candidate versions and their sources. Use it before assuming that a package will come from a particular repository.

For scripts, prefer the documented scripting interfaces such as apt-get and apt-cache, and establish explicit error handling. Do not remove lock files to bypass an active package operation. A merged filesystem layout or package database convention can affect which exact path is recorded. When a file-ownership query fails, inspect the resolved path and package listing before concluding that the file is unmanaged.

Installation should begin with a requirement: which capability is missing, which supported package supplies it, and what services or dependencies will change? After installation, verify the package, configuration, service state, and useful application behavior.

Removal also needs review. A package manager may propose removing dependent packages, and configuration or data may remain according to the command and packaging policy. Inspect the proposed transaction using the manager’s simulation or assume-no facility. Record the package list before and after. For a service, check listeners and residual credentials as well as package state. “Package absent” does not prove “all access and data removed.”

slides.title: 6.9 Updating Systems
keyPoints: Apply updates first in a representative test environment. Include startup, application behavior, data access, and recovery checks. A package transaction completing is only one acceptance condition.
Linux example — 6.9
Preview available updates.
slides.narration:
An update changes a compatible package set and may require service restarts or a reboot. Installing a fixed library does not necessarily replace the copy already mapped into a long-running process. A new kernel package does not replace the running kernel until an appropriate reboot path activates it.

Apply updates first in a representative test environment. Include startup, application behavior, data access, and recovery checks. A package transaction completing is only one acceptance condition.

Classify urgency by exposure, exploitability, available mitigations, and business impact—not merely by how many packages are listed. Security and operations teams should share a decision process for emergency updates. Delaying every update indefinitely creates risk; applying every change without validation creates a different risk.

slides.title: 6.11 Package Verification
keyPoints: On Debian-family systems, dpkg --verify and tools such as debsums can provide checks with their own coverage limits. Consult the installed manual rather than assuming they verify every security property.
Linux example — 6.11

slides.narration:
Package verification compares selected installed-file properties against package metadata. RPM’s rpm -V package can report differences in attributes such as digest, size, mode, and ownership. Changes to configuration files may be expected; unexpected executable changes deserve investigation.

On Debian-family systems, dpkg --verify and tools such as debsums can provide checks with their own coverage limits. Consult the installed manual rather than assuming they verify every security property.

A clean package-verification result is not a complete compromise assessment. An attacker may alter unowned files, runtime state, configuration outside the checked set, or the evidence itself. Use verification as one source of evidence and compare against trusted artifacts when integrity is in question.

slides.title: 6.12 Dependency Problems
keyPoints: Linux example — 6.12
Check dependency consistency.
What to check: Investigate reported conflicts before using force or dependency-bypass options.
slides.narration:
Dependencies express required relationships among packages and versions. A conflict can result from mixed repositories, partial upgrades, held packages, incompatible architectures, or unavailable metadata. Identify the conflict instead of immediately forcing installation.

On Debian-family systems, dpkg --audit can reveal incomplete package state. A reviewed dpkg --configure -a may finish interrupted configuration, and a simulated apt-get -s -f install can show a proposed dependency repair. Read the proposal before allowing removals.

On DNF systems, inspect repository state, installed versions, and the solver’s explanation. Commands such as distribution synchronization can make broad changes and require a planned transaction. Never turn off dependency or signature checking merely to make the error disappear.
